1:
The chapter opens with a confession of difficulty. Adam Clarke says he knows not how to undertake a comment on this psalm, calling it the most difficult in the whole Psalter, and quotes Simon De Muis, that in it there are as many precipices and labyrinths as there are verses or words, so that it may be termed the torture of critics and the reproach of commentators. Keil and Delitzsch concur, quoting Hitzig that it is no easy task to become master of this Titan: the psalm is in the style of Deborah, and all that is most glorious in the earlier literature is concentrated in it. Its language is so peculiarly its own that no fewer than thirteen words occur here and nowhere else.

What occasioned it is equally unsettled. John Calvin reports that most interpreters refer it to the translation of the ark from the house of Obed-Edom to Mount Zion, while others think it penned after some great victory, when the ark was brought back in triumph — and that the ark did accompany the army we learn from Uriah’s words to David. Adam Clarke thinks it probable that part of it was composed by Moses to be recited when the Israelites journeyed, and that David built on that model. Keil and Delitzsch admire the collector’s tact in setting this psalm after the one before, since that began with the echo of Aaron’s benediction and this with the words in which Moses called on the Lord to advance before Israel at Numbers 10:35. Charles Ellicott calls the opening a reminiscence of that battle-cry and points to its later history in Gibbon and in Carlyle on Cromwell.

Whether the first words are petition or prediction is the next question. John Gill reports Kimchi’s answer that it is either prayer or prophecy, and in either case the sense is the same: if a prayer, it is the prayer of faith that so it will be; if a prophecy, it is certain that so it shall be. He refers the arising to Christ’s incarnation or, as many of the ancients took it, to his resurrection. Augustine of Hippo treats the thing as accomplished: Christ has risen up, and his enemies have been dispersed through all nations from the very place where they practised their enmities. Their flight he makes inward, since the flight of the mind is fear — for whither should they flee bodily from the face of him who everywhere shows the efficacy of his presence?

Matthew Henry reads the verse as an exercise in the use of Scripture. David comments upon Moses’s prayer, not only repeating it but enlarging upon it, and so directs us how to make use of scripture-prayers; and it looks further still, to the Redeemer’s victory. He adds that though we are to pray for our own enemies as such, we are to pray against God’s enemies as such. C.H. Spurgeon hears a supposition that the Lord has been passive for a while, suffering his enemies to rage but restraining his power, so that Israel beseeches him to arise as elsewhere to awake and gird on his sword. He has but to arise and they flee, long before the army of Israel can come into the fray.

The two figures of destruction are quickly handled. Charles Ellicott says both the vanishing smoke and the melting wax have occurred before and are too obvious to need any reference to the cloud and fire of the encampment. John Gill makes the smoke describe the character of the wicked as well as the manner of their destruction, as easily brought about as smoke driven by the wind. C.H. Spurgeon takes the answering gladness of the righteous as a duty, since no bounds should be set to joy in the Lord: the presence which is the dread of the wicked is the delight of the saints.
4:
The phrase rendered him that rideth upon the heavens is the first real crux. Charles Ellicott rejects the received rendering as resting on a rabbinical interpretation, since the word by derivation means a dry sandy region, a steppe, its singular with the article naming the Jordan valley. He would read, cast up a highway for him that rideth on the steppes — an apparent echo of Isaiah 40:3, in which the poet’s voice is the herald’s, going before the army of God to order the removal of obstructions and the raising of cairns to mark the road. Such a sense, he adds, suits the allusions to early history that make up so much of the psalm.

Adam Clarke agrees only that the word is of doubtful signification. It comes from a root meaning to mingle, whence the word for twilight, formed of an equal mixture of light and darkness; the Greek and Latin translate it the west. He thinks it probably means the gloomy desert through which God led the Israelites, or else the darkness in which God is said to dwell. Against both he sets the Targum: extol him who sitteth on the throne of glory in the ninth heaven; Jah is his name. John Gill passes over the question and takes the summons as addressed to Christ manifest in the flesh, risen and ascended, who having exerted his great strength in redemption is to be sung the song of redeeming love.

The divine name that follows draws its own notes. Adam Clarke calls it a contraction of the longer name, as the ancient versions understood it, used in only a few places, and says it might be translated the Self-existent. John Wesley adds that the heathens pronounced it Jao, and that rejoicing before him means before the ark, as David danced before the Lord on this occasion. Charles Ellicott renders the clause his name is Jah, notes that this abbreviated form is first found at Exodus 15:2, and concludes that the verse is no doubt a fragment of a song as old as the Exodus — the dependence of this psalm on older songs being nowhere more conspicuous than in its various use of the divine names.

The titles of the fifth verse are handled gently. John Gill takes the father of the fatherless literally, as a character God assumes to express his providence and tenderness, and in which magistrates and all good men should imitate him, caring for them being a branch of pure religion. He then extends it to those deserted by their friends, or called to leave father and mother for Christ’s sake. Charles Ellicott notes that the Greek and Latin prefix a clause here, which seems to indicate that the abrupt introduction of the description is due to some loss in the text, and that these epithets appear to have become almost proverbial very early.

What it means to set the solitary in families divides them again. John Gill reports that the Jewish writers generally understand an increase of families with children in lawful marriage, instancing Abraham and Sarah; the Targum paraphrases it so. Adam Clarke puts the same reading as a question: the word means the single persons, and is not the meaning that God is the author of marriage, and children its lawful fruit an inheritance from him? Charles Ellicott allows that the word might refer to the childless, but thinks it better, with the next clause, to think of the exiles scattered and brought home by the divine arm. The word for chains, he notes, is peculiar to this passage and derived by the Rabbis from a root meaning to bind, though modern scholars give the root as to prosper and would render, he bringeth the captives into prosperity; and the dry land may then be the lot of those left behind in Babylon.
7:
Matthew Henry explains why the psalm turns backward here. Having occasion to thank God for great things lately done, the psalmist praises him for what he did for their fathers of old; fresh mercies should put us in mind of former mercies. The first of these is that God himself was Israel’s guide through the wilderness: when he had brought them out of their chains he did not leave them in the dry land but went before them. And Henry insists on the word — it was not a journey but a march, for they went as soldiers, an army with banners. The Egyptians promised themselves that the wilderness had shut Israel in, but they were deceived, for God’s people, having him for their leader, marched through it and were not lost in it; and if God brings his people into a wilderness he will be sure to go before them in it and bring them out.

C.H. Spurgeon makes the same point against a common way of speaking. We may speak, if we will, of the wanderings of the children of Israel, but we must not think them purposeless strayings: they were in reality a well-arranged and well-considered march. He was Commander-in-chief of Israel, from whom they received all orders, so the march was his march; and because the Lord went before, it mattered nothing whether the Red Sea or burning sand lay in the way, since the pillar of cloud and fire always led them by a right way. John Gill identifies the guide precisely: God went before them in the pillar of cloud and of fire, as the Targum adds, and this divine Person was the Son of God, the Angel of his presence, in whom was the very name mentioned just before. Adam Clarke says only that this verse and the next manifestly refer to the passage of the Israelites through the wilderness.

The Selah at the end of the verse draws a remark from C.H. Spurgeon that none of the others make. This seems an odd place, he says, for a musical pause or direction; but it is better to break a sentence than to spoil praise. The sense is about to be superlatively grand, and the direction therefore intimates as much to the players and singers, that they may perform their parts with suitable solemnity — and it is never untimely, he adds, to remind a congregation that the worship of God should be thoughtfully and heartily presented.

What was shaken at Sinai they describe in much the same terms. Matthew Henry says that never did any people see the glory of God or hear his voice as Israel did, and never had any people such a law given them. Then the earth shook, and the neighbouring countries in all likelihood felt the shock; terrible thunders there were, accompanied no doubt with thunder-showers, in which the heavens seemed to drop, while the divine doctrine dropped as the rain; and Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God. C.H. Spurgeon describes it more briefly — beneath the sublime tread the solid ground trembled, the clouds descended as if the heavens bowed before their God, and that hill, so lone and high, bowed before the manifested God, whom Israel worshipped and who had chosen that nation above all the nations of the earth. John Wesley glosses the dropping as great showers poured down, which accompanied those mighty thunders.

John Gill alone widens the shaking beyond the place. The earth shook not only about Sinai but in other places, he says; and the words may also design the dread and trembling of the inhabitants of the earth when they heard of the wonderful things God did for his people.
9:
What the plentiful rain was is disputed at once. John Gill rules out a series of literal candidates — not water as at the sea, nor the showers that attend thunder and lightning as at the giving of the law, nor the rain of Canaan, nor, as Arama would have it, the rain of manna and quails — and takes it for the effusion of the Holy Spirit, ordinary or extraordinary. That on the day of Pentecost was a plentiful one indeed, and even the ordinary measure of the Spirit’s grace in conversion is exceeding abundant. The Hebrew, he notes, signifies a rain of liberalities, since it comes from the free grace of God and makes those on whom it descends a willing people. Adam Clarke renders the phrase a shower of liberality and takes precisely the reading Gill sets aside, believing it to refer to the manna by which God preserved alive the weary and hungry Israelites. John Wesley keeps to the state of the ground, parched with excessive heat and ready to faint for want of rain.

The congregation of the next verse turns on a single word, which John Gill observes signifies beasts or living creatures. Some understand it of the Gentiles, comparable to such before the gospel came among them; without any limitation it may be applied to all who are quickened by grace, and particularly to gospel ministers, signified by the four living creatures in the visions of Ezekiel and of John. Adam Clarke notes that all the versions render it thy living creature, and asks a question none of the others asks: does this not refer to the quails brought to the camp, which dwelt as it were round about it? Was not this, with the manna and the refreshing rock, the goodness God provided for the poor and needy?

Charles Ellicott offers a third possibility: we may render, thy life dwells in her, that is, in the people of Israel, the vigour consequent on the heavenly food being called the divine life, which would conceal a higher application. John Wesley keeps to the plain sense throughout: the congregation is the people of Israel, and the land is what God gave for their use, expelling the old inhabitants and making it fruitful by his special blessing; they were poor indeed when he undertook to conduct them into Canaan.
11:
Who published the word, and what the word was, is the sharpest disagreement in the psalm. John Gill takes it of the gospel: the Lord committed the word of reconciliation to his apostles as a sacred trust, gave them gifts qualifying them for its ministration and a door of utterance to speak it, and the Targum wrongly interprets it of the word of the law. Charles Ellicott names that reading and rejects it. Literally, he says, the line runs, the Lord gives a word; of the women who bring the news, the host is great. The Hebrew for a word is poetical and used especially of a divine utterance, and might mean either the signal for the conflict or the announcement of victory; but the custom of granting to bands of maidens the privilege of celebrating a triumph makes for the latter. And it is the Greek and Latin renderings, he adds, that are the source of the erroneous view making this verse prophetic of a numerous and successful Christian ministry.

Adam Clarke reads the clause the same way and gives it flatly: of the female preachers there was a great host, which he calls the literal translation, leaving the reader to make of it what he pleases. The publication of good news belonged to the women, who announced it to the people at large, and to this universal custom the psalmist alludes. C.H. Spurgeon stages the scene: the silver trumpet from the tabernacle door was God’s mouth to warn the camp, and then was there hurrying to and fro, the ten thousand maids of Israel running from tent to tent to bid the valiant men hasten to the fray. He turns it at once into a wish — O for the like zeal in the church today, that when the gospel is published both men and women may eagerly spread the glad tidings. Charles Ellicott presses further: not one body of women celebrating one victory, but successive tidings following rapidly on one another, thick as tale came post with post. This verse and the two that follow wear the air of a fragment of those ancient battle-songs sung by the women after the defeat of the foe, torn from a context whose loss accounts for their great obscurity.

The flight of the kings is described in much the same terms by all of them, and identified differently. John Gill takes them for the enemies of the gospel, Roman emperors who fled before it at the downfall of Paganism, calling on the mountains to hide them from Christ. Adam Clarke and John Wesley keep to the older history, naming the kings of Canaan and the nations who came against Israel with great armies. Keil and Delitzsch hear irony in the phrase itself: kings of hosts sounds like a disparaging antithesis to the title of the Lord of hosts. He interposes, and they are obliged to flee, staggering as they go, far away in every direction.

The woman who stayed behind draws the last comment. Keil and Delitzsch take her collectively for the wife who remains at home while the husband goes forth to battle, and reject the alternative that Luther adopted with the Greek, Latin and Syriac, which makes the phrase the ornament of the house. Charles Ellicott agrees that the Hebrew means the woman keeping the house, but observes that though the picture of women waiting for the victorious home-coming is true to life, the next verse indicates a latent reference to some tribe who shirked the battle and played the stay-at-home. Adam Clarke identifies her outright as Deborah the prophetess, accustomed to tarry at home and take care of the family, who divided the spoils. C.H. Spurgeon makes the division a mark of the completeness of the rout: the feeblest in Israel had a portion of the prey, and gallant warriors cast their spoils at the women’s feet.
13:
The obscure line about lying among the pots draws three quite different addresses. John Gill reports without settling. Kimchi takes it for a word to Israelites going out to war, who though they should lie in a low, dark and disagreeable place, exposed to wind and weather, should yet be fair and beautiful and loaded with the gold and silver of the enemy. Fortunatus Scacchus refers it, much better in Gill’s judgment, to the order of the army going to battle — the body in the middle and the two wings on either side, their glittering armour of gold and brass taking the rays of the sun, fitly resembled by the colours on the wings and back of a dove. A third writer takes the words as an address to the dove itself, meaning the Holy Spirit, expostulating how long he would dwell within the borders of Canaan. Adam Clarke hears no dove but a reproach: the prophet addresses the tribes of Reuben and Gad, who remained in their inheritance with their domestic affairs while the other tribes went against Jabin and the Canaanitish kings. You were thus occupied while your brethren sustained a desperate campaign; you are inglorious, and they dwell under the rich tents they took from the enemy. John Wesley keeps it general: you have formerly been exposed to great reproach and misery, yet God has changed your condition.

On the colours the two agree. John Wesley has them beautiful and glorious, like the feathers of a dove, which according to the variety of its postures and of the light shining on it look like silver and gold. Adam Clarke presses the Hebrew: the phrase means native gold, so splendidly yellow as to approach greenness, the doubling of the last syllable denoting excess — excessively green, blistering green.

Clarke then sets down what he calls a curious Targum paraphrase of both verses, in which the congregation of Israel, like a dove covered with the clouds of glory, divides the prey of the Egyptians, and stretching out its hands in prayer over the sea sees the Almighty cast down kingdoms and cool hell like snow. Perhaps the Romanists, he remarks, got some idea of purgatory here: for the sake of the righteous the flames of hell are extinguished.

Who the scattered kings are is left open by John Gill in the same way he left the pots. They may be the ministers and preachers God gives in large numbers, spiritual governors set over churches, which is how Jarchi read them in speaking of the disciples of the wise men; or those made kings and priests unto God; or wicked kings destroyed by the dove, the church, at the battle of Armageddon. John Wesley stays with the conquest: it was in Canaan, at the coming of the Israelites, and the land was left as white as the snow on Salmon.
15:
Whether Zion is being compared with Bashan or set against it divides the entry. John Gill compares: the church is the hill of God, an excellent and supereminent one in which he dwells, called a hill for its visibility, and likened to Bashan for fertility and fruitfulness — hence the kine and bulls, the rams and lambs and fatlings of Bashan, and the oaks thereof; the ordinances of the church are green pastures where his people become fat and flourishing. C.H. Spurgeon denies it outright: it does not appear that Zion is compared with Bashan but contrasted with it. Zion was not a high hill comparatively, and he concedes Bashan the greater mount, but not the more glorious, since in choosing Zion the Lord exalted it above the loftier hills. The loftiness of nature is nothing before him; he passes by the proud uplifted peaks and makes the base things of this world monuments of his grace and sovereignty. He adds a note on the idiom: by Hebrew custom every great or remarkable thing is called after God, as the trees of the Lord and the river of God — where English says the Devil’s Dyke, the Devil’s Ditch, the Devil’s Punch Bowl, the more commendable idiom of the Hebrews says the hill of God.

Matthew Henry agrees, and makes the point moral: Zion was little and low beside them and not covered over with flocks and herds as they were, yet has the pre-eminence above them all because it is the hill God desires to dwell in. It is much more honourable, he says, to be holy to God than to be high and great in the world. Though you exceed it in bulk and be first-rates, he has Zion answer the high hills, yet because on this the royal flag is hoisted you must all strike sail to it. John Wesley says the height meant is not external but spiritual, the exaltation of God’s presence and worship. Adam Clarke reaches the same sense by repunctuating both verses as questions — Is Mount Bashan the craggy mount, the mount of God? Why envy ye, ye craggy mounts? — and cites the Targum, which has Moriah chosen for the sanctuary and Sinai for the giving of the law while Bashan, Tabor and Carmel are rejected.

Charles Ellicott reads the names geographically: mountain of God, mount Bashan; mountain of peaks, mount Bashan. The basalt ranges — basanite, he notes, probably from the locality — always rise before the eyes of those looking eastward from Palestine, doubly impressive for their superior height and for the contrast of their bold and rugged outlines with the monotonous rounded limestone hills to the west; the term might take in all the heights east of Jordan, which would add propriety to their being introduced as jealously watching the march of Israel. Why they are called mountains of God has been much discussed: some take it for ancient seats of religious worship, others simply for grandeur, a ridge of god-like greatness.

The strange verb in the next verse occurs nowhere else, and the roster splits over it. Charles Ellicott takes it, by comparison with an Arabic root, for a beast crouching to spring on its prey — the jealous hills lying like panthers ready to spring on the passing Israelites, an image he supports out of Browning — while allowing that others make it simply to look enviously, and that the older versions caught the sense as watching with suspicion. John Gill gathers the same Arabic evidence from the rabbis, that the word signifies to lie in wait, and to look out and leap upon the prey, and applies it to the kingdoms of this world that lie in wait for the church and insult over it in vain. John Wesley takes it flatly as triumphing and looking upon Zion with contempt.
17:
The number is the first difficulty. John Gill takes the chariots for angels, so called because they have appeared in that form, because like chariots of war they are the strength and protection of the Lord’s people, and because of their swiftness in doing his work; they are the chariots in which Christ ascended, in which he will descend at the last day, and in which he now fetches the souls of his people to him at death. Their number is put at twenty thousand here and greater elsewhere, and is observed both for the glory of God and for the safety of his people. John Wesley makes it a round figure, a certain number put for an uncertain, the armies which attend upon God to do his pleasure. Adam Clarke does the arithmetic instead: two myriads of thousands doubled — does not this mean simply forty thousand? He sets down the Targum, which has two thousand angels drawing the chariots and the majesty of God resting upon them in holiness on Sinai, and then stops: but what does this mean? We must die to know.

Charles Ellicott finds the verse unusable as it stands. Its literal reading can only be brought into harmony with the context by a certain violence to grammar, since by strict rule it must mean that the Lord rides in his innumerable chariots to Sinai — and the whole tenor of the passage describes a march from Sinai, not to it. The proposal that the Lord is among them, a Sinai in holiness, meaning that Zion has become Sinai, he grants is a common enough figure in poetry but is only discovered here by a roundabout process; he prefers the emendation of Perowne, that the Lord is with them and has come from Sinai into the holy place. As for the angels, that rendering arose from confusing the word meaning repetition with a word meaning shining, and the Greek and Latin versions have flourishing ones and rejoicing ones. But the mistake is a happy one, and he lets Milton keep it, quoting the lines of Paradise Lost in which cherub and seraph, potentates and thrones are poured about the numberless chariots.

On the ascent the older reading is unanimous and the newer one is not. John Gill rules out the alternatives one by one — not Moses ascending to the firmament, as the Targum and Jarchi have it, of which we nowhere read; not David going up to the high fortresses, as Aben Ezra; not God’s ascent from Sinai — and settles on Christ’s ascension, which was not figurative but real and local, from earth to heaven, certain and visible, seen to go up by angels and men, and so expressed in the past tense though it was then future. John Wesley agrees that it is literally accomplished in Christ alone, while allowing that the language is borrowed from the ancient custom of princes going up into their royal cities in triumphant chariots attended by their captive enemies. Adam Clarke starts from that custom and stays with it: the ark has reached the top of Zion, the conqueror is placed on a very elevated chariot, the conquered kings and generals walk bound behind it, and money is thrown among the crowd. Charles Ellicott keeps it earthbound throughout — on high means to the height, Mount Zion — and rejects the received rendering of the gifts outright. For men is inadmissible; the Hebrew is in man, equivalent to of men, so that the gifts are the captives or hostages themselves, the rebellious of the next clause, the heathen subjected to the Lord and their land made his dwelling-place. John Wesley takes the gifts as all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge received according to Christ’s manhood, and Adam Clarke hears in the phrase that God manifest in the flesh dwells among mortals.
19:
Whether God loads us or carries us turns on one Hebrew verb, and the roster works through every option. John Gill lays them side by side: Aben Ezra and Kimchi supply the word blessings, which gives the familiar reading that he daily loads us with benefits, spiritual and temporal; but the words may as well be rendered that he will bear us, as a father his child or a shepherd his lambs, and so he does from the womb even to hoary hairs; or again that he will put a burden upon us, meaning afflictions, which are of the Lord’s laying, though he will lay no more upon his people than he will enable them to bear. The Targum, he adds, interprets it of the burdensomeness of the law. Keil and Delitzsch settle it on the accents, following the pointing restored by Baer after Heidenheim, which yields blessed be the Lord: daily he bears for us, and note that the Targum, Rashi and Kimchi agree; the verb, like its neighbours, unites the sense of laying a burden on someone with that of carrying one. Charles Ellicott observes that the italics of the Authorised Version already confess the difficulty: the verb has both an active and a passive sense, and the context seems to require the latter, that he daily takes our burden for us, whether the burden of trial or of sin — though it is quite possible, he allows, to render that if any put a burden on us, God is our help.

Adam Clarke is not content to canvass. With benefits, he says, is not in the text, and he sets out what the versions offer instead: the Vulgate, Septuagint and Arabic make God the one who makes our journey prosperous, the Syriac the one who has chosen our inheritance, while the verb itself signifies to lift, bear up, support, or bear a burden for another. His own rendering is that God bears our burdens for us day by day. Then the verdict: but loadeth us with benefits is neither a translation nor meaning.

The issues from death divide the same way, between escape and source. John Wesley glosses them in two words as escapes or deliverances. C.H. Spurgeon fills that out: the Almighty who has entered into covenant with us is the source of our safety, and when his children are at their wit’s end and see no way out he can find them a door; the gates of the grave none can open but himself, and on the heavenward side he has set the doors open for all his people. John Gill keeps to the first clause, reading it as God for us, on our side, the mighty God able to save to the uttermost. Adam Clarke hears the exodus in the phrase, the going out from death, from the land of Egypt and the house of bondage, and offers as an alternative that life and death are simply in the hand of God, who can create and destroy. Charles Ellicott refuses to choose. Literally the Hebrew is for death goings out, and the same word elsewhere means sources; so the sense depends on whether the clause is joined to what precedes or to what follows, and the verse may mean that the Lord would provide an issue out of death for Israel and a source of death to Israel’s enemies. The Greek and Latin, he notes, apparently take it the first way.
21:
The wounded head is read at two levels. John Gill takes it of the chief of God’s enemies, Satan the prince of devils and the god of this world, and notes that to wound here is the same as to bruise, which is how the Targum has it. The hairy scalp then puzzles everyone. Adam Clarke asks outright whether the phrase means anything like the Indian scalping, or whether it refers to a crest on a helmet or headcap, and supposes the latter. John Wesley keeps it on the enemy’s own head: in ancient times many people used to wear long and shaggy hair, that their looks might be more terrible to their enemies. Charles Ellicott reads it literally as crown, or top, or head of hair, the word rendered pate elsewhere in the Psalms, and thinks it probably a portrait of some historical person hostile to Israel, though others take it as a type of pride and arrogance on the analogy of a Greek verb for wearing the hair long. He adds a note on the English: scalp, properly a shell, was a word in common use when the English Bible was translated, and he quotes a line of Richard II in which white beards have armed their thin and hairless scalps against the king’s majesty.

What deliverance is promised from Bashan and the depths of the sea divides the entry more sharply. Matthew Henry hears the old ones promised again: God will bring them from the depths of the sea as he brought Israel out of the slavery of Egypt into the ease and liberty of the wilderness, and from Bashan as he brought them out of their wants and wanderings into the fulness and settlement of Canaan, that land beyond Jordan where they had their wars with Sihon and Og. The former appearances of God’s power and goodness, he says, should encourage faith and hope for the future, that what he has done he will do again, and we may perhaps see repeated all the wonders our fathers told us of. John Wesley says the same in a sentence, and Adam Clarke narrows it to the defeat of the Egyptians and the miraculous passage of the Red Sea. Charles Ellicott calls the meaning very obscure and will not tie it to the exodus at all: it is plainly another fragment of some ancient song, quoted, he can hardly doubt, with reference to the return from captivity, in which Bashan and the depths of the sea may stand generally for east and west, the sea being the Mediterranean — though the original verse, he grants, most probably did refer to the Red Sea and the contest with the king of Bashan.

The blood in which the foot is dipped is read as consequence, as history, and as syntax. John Gill ties the verse back to the wounding, to be read with the intervening words in a parenthesis: the Messiah would so wound the head of his people’s enemies that there should be an effusion of blood large enough for their feet to be dipped in it. Adam Clarke makes it the slaughter of the Amorites, so great that thou shalt walk over their dead bodies while beasts of prey feed upon them. Matthew Henry recalls that dogs licked the blood of Ahab, and treats the victories God gave David’s forces as types of Christ’s victory over death and the grave. Charles Ellicott objects that the Authorised Version makes an unnecessary transposition of a very involved sentence; the image is perfectly clear, though the syntax, as often happens in all languages, goes tripping itself up. The conqueror, after wading in the blood of his enemies, is met by the dogs, who lick his gory feet — and with the change of a single letter the line may be rendered that thou mayest wash thy foot in blood.
24:
Everyone agrees a procession is being described; they differ over who is watching it and who is in it. John Wesley keeps it plain: men saw and observed the carrying of the ark to Zion, the solemnity of which the following verses describe, and the sanctuary is the tabernacle prepared for it. Charles Ellicott tightens the words — goings is better rendered processions, and in the sanctuary rather into the sanctuary. Adam Clarke puts the spectators outside Israel altogether: it is the kings of the Amorites who have seen God’s terrible majesty, in their own discomfiture and the slaughter of their subjects. John Gill makes the goings themselves the saving of God’s people and the destroying of his enemies. C.H. Spurgeon sets the scene at the moment of arrival, the procession climbing the hill and entering the enclosure where the tabernacle of the ark was pitched, and then widens it as far as it will go: all nature and providence are a procession attending the great Lord in his visitations of this lower globe, winter and summer, sun and moon, storm and calm swelling the pomp of the King of kings.

On the order of the march C.H. Spurgeon finds a rule — singers first and musicians after, for the song must lead the music and not the music drown the singing — while declining the inference some have drawn from it, that vocal music is superior to instrumental, on the ground that we need not go so far for arguments. John Gill hears the apostles and ministers of the word in the singers, the gospel being a joyful sound and like vocal music harmonious and delightful, and thinks the allusion is to singers going before armies marching to battle or returning with victory. Charles Ellicott identifies the instruments instead: the players are harpers, and the damsels are beating the tambourine. Adam Clarke says only that the verse appears to be a description of the procession.

The fountain of Israel and little Benjamin then draw the sharpest split in the entry. John Wesley takes the fountain for all the people of Israel, and Benjamin for the tribe, called little because it was exceedingly diminished and almost extinguished under the judges, and named here as the tribe which had lately swayed the sceptre but now submitted to David; Zebulun and Naphtali are mentioned because they lived in the remotest parts of Canaan, so that by naming two of the nearest tribes and two of the farthest the psalmist intimates that all the rest came too. Charles Ellicott agrees the procession is a representative one and thinks Zebulun and Naphtali were chosen for their prominence in Deborah’s song, Benjamin for giving the nation its first king, and Judah as the tribe of David — possibly the four standing for the two kingdoms. Their ruler, he adds, translates a word that always carries the sense of a high-handed conqueror’s rule, which points again to Saul; and their council must be corrected to their crowd, or company. On the fountain he allows that the congregations may be understood as sprung from the head waters of the races, the patriarchal ancestors, but adds that if there were any mode of taking the words literally instead of figuratively it would be preferable. John Gill denies it is the tribe at all. The Targum and Jarchi read it so, but he takes little Benjamin for the Apostle Paul, who was of that tribe, a young man when converted as the Septuagint and Vulgate have it here, little in stature as is generally reported of him and as his name may be thought to signify, and little in his own eyes.
28:
Whether the first line states a fact or asks a favour is settled differently by one voice than by the rest. John Wesley reads it as done: God has ordained or effectually procured all that strength which Israel has put forth at any time. C.H. Spurgeon reads it the same way and presses it: the decree had ordained the nation strong and the arm of God had made them so, and as a commander-in-chief the Lord made the valiant men pass in battle array and bade them be strong in the day of conflict. He turns the second clause into the pattern of Christian prayer — as all power comes from God at first, so its continual maintenance is also of him, and we who have life should pray to have it more abundantly, expecting God to bless his own work, since he has never left any work unfinished yet and never will. John Gill hesitates over the addressee rather than the mood, taking the words either for an apostrophe to the Messiah, whose Father had sent out the rod of his strength from Zion into Judea and the Gentile world, or for a word to the churches and their rulers, that as their day was so their strength should be. Charles Ellicott repoints the whole line: rather, with the Greek and the ancient versions generally, Ordain, O God, thy strength. Adam Clarke notes only that this and the verses following are what the procession sang.

Which temple is meant then divides them three ways. John Wesley takes it for the temple Solomon would build, and the kings for kings of the Gentiles, which happened in part in the days of Solomon and Hezekiah and more fully when the Lord came into his temple. C.H. Spurgeon keeps the same history and adds the detail: the palace of God towering above Jerusalem was prophesied to become a wonder to all lands, and when it grew from the tabernacle of David to the temple of Solomon it was so, splendid enough that the queen of far-off Sheba came with her gifts and neighbouring princes brought tribute. Charles Ellicott turns the verse into evidence about the psalm’s date, calling it a strong argument for referring the whole composition either to the time of the rebuilding of the Temple or to its re-dedication after the pollution by Antiochus Epiphanes. John Gill denies that any building is in view. The material temple was not in being in David’s time; it was built by his son and destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, rebuilt by Zerubbabel and repaired by Herod, and though the Messiah entered it as its Lord and proprietor it was quickly after demolished, and, he says, will never be rebuilt more. What is meant is the spiritual temple of which Christ is builder, foundation and cornerstone and believers are the materials, and the Jerusalem is the heavenly one, the mother of us all. Matthew Henry takes the verses as an invitation rather than a description: there is beauty and benefit enough in the service of God to invite sinners out of all nations, and some will submit from fear, overcome by their consciences and the checks of Providence, while others submit willingly.
30:
Almost everyone thinks the Authorised Version has the wrong creature here. Adam Clarke says so outright: the Hebrew means the wild beast of the reed, the crocodile or hippopotamus, the emblem of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and thus all the versions have it; our translators have mistaken the meaning, though they have put the true sense in the margin. Charles Ellicott agrees, sending the reader to that margin and noting that with beasts changed to beast it gives the right rendering; the beast of the reed is undoubtedly symbolical of Egypt. John Gill canvasses first — some rabbis take the word for men who fight with spears slender as reeds, and Aben Ezra says spears are so called in Arabic — but he too prefers the beast, thinking of the lions in the thickets of Jordan, the behemoth lying under the covert of reeds, the crocodile of the Nile, perhaps the river horse, and taking the figure for an insidious, cruel and tyrannical prince such as Pharaoh. John Wesley passes over the reed altogether and reads the verse as a chastisement of those who will not bring presents, the bulls being the fierce and furious adversaries of God and his church and the calves the people or soldiers depending on them.

Charles Ellicott keeps working at the grammar after the others have stopped. The bulls and calves may stand for the strong and the weak, princes and common people, and a slight emendation would give the herd of bulls as despisers of the people; the bull-worship of Egypt makes the figure especially significant. The clause about submitting, he says, still waits for a satisfactory explanation: the Authorised Version is intelligible but grammatically indefensible, the Greek is undoubtedly right to take the verb as a contracted infinitive after a negative, and the sense submit is only with violence deduced from a root that means to stamp like a furious animal — one cognate being used of a herd fouling the pasture with their feet. His own rendering has the rebuke fall on those who march for pieces of silver, that is, not on Egypt only but on the Jews who took Egyptian pay as mercenaries and oppressed the rest of the community.

What Egypt and Ethiopia then do is dated four ways. Adam Clarke finds a literal fulfilment under Solomon, in the alliance sealed by his marriage and in the queen of Sheba coming to Jerusalem, and a second after the resurrection: there were Egyptians at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost who, Hilary tells us, on their return proclaimed what they had seen and became the ambassadors of Christ in that country, and the Ethiopian eunuch was among the first Gentiles to receive the gospel. The Hebrew is very emphatic, he adds — Cush will cause her hands to run out to God — and the Chaldee paraphrases it well, that the sons of Cush will run that they may spread out their hands in prayer. Charles Ellicott reads the same idiom as expressing simply hasty submission, and renders princes as magnates. John Wesley takes the two names for the ancient enemies of God and understands by them all other nations of the like character, begging mercy of him; the prophecy, he says, evidently belongs to the times of the Messiah. John Gill makes it the conversion of the Gentiles in the latter day, when the kings of the earth become Christians and antichrist is destroyed — unless, he offers, we understand it of kings and princes leaving the communion of the church of Rome, which is spiritually and mystically Egypt. The conversion of every sinner, he ends, is a coming out of Egypt, a call out of darkness and bondage worse than that of Egypt into light and liberty.
32:
The closing call goes out to the whole earth, and the roster differs mainly in how far it reaches. John Gill takes the kingdoms for all of them, Papal, Pagan and Mahometan alike, converted to Christ and singing for their deliverance from the darkness and delusions they were formerly under. Matthew Henry reads the invitation as the sequel to the prophecy just made, the Gentiles now called in to join the devout Israelites, and sets out three grounds of praise: God’s supreme and sovereign dominion, his awful and terrible majesty, and his mighty power, which it is folly to contend with and wisdom to submit to. Adam Clarke says simply that all the inhabitants of the earth are invited. C.H. Spurgeon makes the scale of the choir the point — glorious shall that song be in which whole empires join — and draws a rule from it: so sweet a thing is song that it ought to be all the Lord’s, a secular concert being almost a sacrilege and a licentious song treason. Charles Ellicott attends to the words instead, preferring play and sing, and remarks that the Selah is introduced here, as in some other cases, where to our sense of rhythm it is quite out of place.

What the mighty voice is divides them. Matthew Henry takes it for thunder, which is called the voice of the Lord and said to be full of majesty, or in particular for that thunder in which God spoke to Israel at Sinai. Adam Clarke keeps it in the sky and makes it a word of command: God manages the heavens as an able and skilful rider manages his horse, and at his order the sun, moon and planets run and shed or reflect their light without the smallest deviation; the strength in the clouds is the bursting and pounding of thunder and lightning, which all nations have taken for an especial manifestation of his sovereignty. C.H. Spurgeon hears one clap in particular and asks whether a thunder-clap was just then heard in heaven. John Wesley alone takes it of the gospel, published by Christ and his apostles and assisted by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, which might well be called a mighty voice because it produced such great and wonderful effects; and he catches what the ancient heavens are set against — they are of old, from the beginning of the world, whereas the ark was only some hundreds of years old. John Gill reads the ride as Christ’s ascension far above all heavens, and notes that since he went up from Olivet, east of Jerusalem, the alternative rendering eastward suits it. C.H. Spurgeon sets the two halves of the psalm side by side: before, God was described in his earthly manifestations, marching through the desert; now, in his celestial glory, riding in the heavens of the primeval ages, whose splendours stood fast before men or angels were created.

The last verse is terrible or reverend according to who is reading. Adam Clarke takes the holy places for the sanctuary and heaven, out of the one shining forth with consuming splendour as in the case of Korah, out of the other appearing in storms and thunder; and he ends in doxology, that God alone is worthy to be worshipped, since without him nothing is wise, nothing holy, nothing strong, and from him as the inexhaustible fountain all good must be derived. Charles Ellicott reduces the plural to a single place, Zion. John Gill hears judgment in the word, vengeance on antichrist and the antichristian states, but allows that it may be rendered reverend, to be feared and worshipped by his saints. John Wesley glosses it in three words as deservedly to be feared, and Matthew Henry asks the reader to acknowledge a power sufficient both to protect God’s faithful subjects and to destroy his stubborn adversaries.
